rationale: No panel dissent is present in the packet. The judgment changed in treatment, not in verdict, so a complete assessment is returned. Since the incumbent, the ledger has taken in the proponents' own account of their Pumapunku fieldwork (GEO-E057 to GEO-E066) and the corrected title of GEO-E006, which shows that the Materials Letters paper analysed red sandstone (sample PP4, slab No. 2), so only the Ceramics International paper concerns andesite — and its sample PP1 was picked by its flat surface from loose debris outside the protected monument area (GEO-E057), analysed with no natural andesite comparator (GEO-E060), with nitrogen only semi-quantitative and the authors unable to say whether the organic matter is unreacted guano or a binder (GEO-E059); the interior subsample PP1C (GEO-E058) is the strongest surviving part of the result, and the promised radiocarbon date has not been located (GEO-E066). The verdicts on GEO-C004 (well_supported: the papers do report what the claim says) and GEO-C021 (weakly_supported: positive records from one interested team, no independent negative) hold, but their strongest objections, diagnosticity summaries and what-would-change-our-mind lists now name those records, which is a change of treatment. GEO-C913 and GEO-C918 are added to the featured set (22 featured) because the identity of PP1 is now the sample-provenance crux of the branch the case verdict turns on; GEO-C004 is added to the load-bearing set because the case is unresolved rather than contradicted only on the strength of the positive Andean record it names. The case verdict unresolved stands: Egypt is contradicted where tested with binder-aware methods, the Andes are positive from one team and untested by anyone else, and an existential thesis is neither refuted by one failed instance nor supported by an untested one. Crux order now leads with GEO-R016 (establish what PP1 is and test a documented fragment), then GEO-R009 and GEO-R012, and adds GEO-R015, GEO-R017, GEO-R018, GEO-R019 and GEO-R014. The article's Andean section is rewritten so the reader learns what was sampled and what the analysts concede, with the two new claims spanned; the salt, Egyptian and Aswan sections stand on the same records as before; all five plates are kept in place.
article:
At the granite quarries of Aswan, beside the largest abandoned obelisk in Egypt, there is a block that tourists are invited to hit. The idea is charming: pick up one of the rounded dolerite stones that ancient workers supposedly used, strike the granite, and feel the past in your hands. Guides have been running this accidental experiment for decades. According to the proponent literature, [no visitor has ever managed to reproduce one of the smooth, scooped depressions that cover the quarry walls]{claim=GEO-C002}. The stones bounce. The granite shrugs.

{plate:IMG-GEO-P01}

Anecdotes like this prove nothing by themselves, and this one has never been systematically surveyed — nobody has counted the attempts, weighed the effort, or examined the test block for wear. But it points at the right question, which is not *who built the monuments* — nobody serious disputes that ancient Egyptians built the pyramids and ancient Andeans built Tiwanaku — but *how the hardest stone was worked*. The megalithic casting hypothesis gives a heterodox answer: some of it was not worked at all. It was made — mixed, moulded, and set in place, the way we make concrete — from crushed or gathered rock, a mineral binder, and chemistry that a Bronze Age society could plausibly command.

{plate:IMG-GEO-P02}

The idea has a serious pedigree and a disreputable neighbourhood. It was put in scientific form by the French materials chemist Joseph Davidovits, whose group has since published in peer-reviewed materials journals, and it has attracted at least one laboratory with no stake in the theory. It also circulates in a media ecosystem of lost civilisations and ancient high technology that this case has nothing to do with. Casting requires no aliens, no Atlantis, and no forgotten machines — only forgotten chemistry, which is a documented historical phenomenon. That is what makes it testable. And it has been tested — at one monument thoroughly, at another not at all. The two records are different, and the difference is the whole story.

## The conventional account, taken seriously

Any honest map of this dispute starts by steelmanning the orthodoxy, because the orthodoxy is strong.

The carved-and-transported account is not a guess. Quarries exist, with unfinished monuments still attached to bedrock — the Aswan obelisk itself is the most famous, abandoned mid-extraction after the granite cracked. Tools have been recovered in quantity. Worker settlements at Giza have been excavated. Radiocarbon dates on organic material from the Old Kingdom monuments — much of it charcoal burned in preparing mortar — place the Great Pyramid in the historical era, though the dates run centuries older than the textbook chronology, an offset the dating project attributes to old wood recycled as fuel. Experimental archaeologists have carved granite with dolerite and copper, slowly but genuinely. And modern geochemical provenancing has matched monument stone to specific quarries. The cleanest example is Stonehenge: immobile-trace-element analysis finds that fifty of fifty-two sarsens share a single geochemical profile, and Stone 58's signature directly matches the West Woods area about 25 km away — not a loose statistical resemblance but a match.

The conventional account's gaps are quantitative, not existential. It needs no miracle anywhere. What it needs, in a few specific places, is more time, more workers, or better technique than anyone has yet demonstrated. Those places are where this case lives.

## Where the anomalies actually are

Strip away everything anecdotal and the residue is small but real. It comes in three kinds: rates, ingredients, and the record. A fourth — the salt on the pyramid's walls — gets its own section, because it is the anomaly on which the evidence is thick enough to reach a conclusion.

### Rates

For a century the standard account of granite quarrying rested largely on Reginald Engelbach's 1922 report on the Aswan obelisk. Proponents characterise [its experimental basis as a single self-conducted one-hour trial with no measurement of the mass removed, and its workforce figure as a heuristic read off groove spacing]{claim=GEO-C502}; that characterisation is theirs and has not been checked against the monograph — and the same author's characterisations of three other sources have been found to differ from the originals — so hold it loosely. In 2023 a team finally produced a modern number: [photogrammetric measurement of granite removal with a dolerite pounder gave roughly 216 cubic centimetres per hour at 85 strikes a minute]{claim=GEO-C001} — a rate the authors themselves say speaks against pounders as the *sole* quarrying method. That is a peer-reviewed measurement, from a single team, and it is the most mainstream-legible item in the anomaly column.

Note carefully what it is evidence *for*. It stresses the orthodox timeline. It says nothing about casting: fire-setting, chisels, or simply more labour would each absorb the shortfall without a single mould. Nor are the pounders themselves mysterious. A survey of the Aswan quarries by Egyptian antiquities inspectors and a Norwegian geologist finds that the dolerite came from dykes within the local granite, and identifies trenches cut into such dykes in the Northern quarries — with roughly shaped blanks of pounder size lying beside them — as Pharaonic tool-production quarries, the closest yet found to the Unfinished Obelisk; another candidate lies beside the temple entrance at Philae. That is a local pounder industry embedded in the quarry landscape, and it weighs against the proponents' picture of hundreds of dolerite spheres carried in for some purpose other than striking granite — though the survey describes the wear on the tools only qualitatively, does not itself test what they struck, and Engelbach in 1922 thought the stone did not occur locally, a disagreement nobody has settled. The quarry's stranger features sit in the same unmeasured condition — [vertical shafts some five metres deep, described as too narrow for a worker to swing a pounder at their bottom]{claim=GEO-C006} — surveyed by nobody without a stake in the answer. The conventional reading takes them for test shafts sunk to prove the granite before the trench was cut; the casting reading takes them for processing vessels. Both are conjecture until someone records their geometry and swabs their floors for residues.

### Ingredients

The natron-route version of the hypothesis, developed by the researcher Marcell Fóti, starts from a fact that is not in dispute: Egypt sat on [industrial-scale deposits of natron — the alkaline salt ancient glassmakers used as a flux — exploited from antiquity, with supply declining sharply in the seventh to ninth centuries AD]{claim=GEO-C011}. Natron plus heat plus silica gives waterglass, a mineral binder, and [the roughly 850 °C required was within reach of charcoal-and-bellows pyrotechnology]{claim=GEO-C010} — a point the record supports only through a proponent's citation of early glassmaking, though what is known of ancient metallurgy makes it hard to doubt. Crucible-scale heat, however, is not industrial-scale processing, and the natron papers concern glass and faience; they say nothing about stone. The proposed discovery story — that [long-used outdoor fire pits accidentally produce hardened artificial stone through ash chemistry]{claim=GEO-C013} — rests on one unattributed anecdote and has never been replicated.

All of this is necessary for casting and none of it is evidence of casting. Ingredients on the shelf do not make a cake.

### The record

{plate:IMG-GEO-P05}

The historical anchors are thin. In the Tomb of Rekhmire an 18th-Dynasty mural shows a large casting operation — rows of crucibles tended by workers with poles. Egyptology reads it as bronze casting. Fóti argues that [the scale and apparatus depicted fit mineral or waterglass processing better than bronze work]{claim=GEO-C005}. That is an interpretive argument by a proponent that conventional Egyptology has not engaged; a serious re-reading would ask what residues or tools each interpretation predicts in the archaeological record, and go and look.

## The salt

The proponents' favourite historical anchor is a story about the Caliph al-Maʾmūn. When his party broke into the Great Pyramid in the ninth century, the story goes, [it found the interior chamber walls coated with a layer of salt]{claim=GEO-C003} — a centimetre and a half of cooking salt, in the Geopolymer Institute's telling. Salt is an odd thing for a sealed structure of dry quarried limestone to produce, and an expected residue of stone that set wet with natron in it. The Institute adds a modern coda: on four visits between 1984 and 2003 Davidovits picked up fragments at Giza and found them salty to the tongue, European cathedrals are not salt-encrusted, and so [Great Pyramid stone carries surface salt that comparable natural limestone does not]{claim=GEO-C506}.

Take the medieval story first. The principal Arabic accounts of the breach were gathered in the fifteenth century by al-Suyūṭī, whose compilation exists in Leon Nemoy's 1939 translation. It tells the story twice, and in detail. The workers kindled fire, applied vinegar, tempered iron tools and brought up catapults; they found the wall twenty cubits thick; behind it a jar holding a thousand dinars, a square well with doors onto chambers of shrouded corpses, a narrow shaft of black quartz, a covered granite basin in which they found “nothing but worn out pieces of rope”. Not one of these passages mentions salt, halite, or any coating on the walls. The web page that carries the salt report names no medieval author, work or manuscript for it. Even its date is unsupported: the translator places the caliph's arrival in Egypt, to suppress a rebellion, in AH 217 — that is AD 832, not the 820 the page gives. Other medieval authors remain to be read, and a single located passage would revive the story. But on what has been read, the claim that the accounts report salt is not merely unproven: the accounts that exist do not report it, and the only text that says they do cites nothing. We grade it contradicted, with low confidence, and name the unread authors as the way to reverse that.

Now the modern salt — which turns out to be real. A conservation study by the ScanPyramids mission, published in *Scientific Reports* in 2026, examined efflorescence (the white crust that forms when dissolved salts migrate to a surface and crystallise) inside the Queen's Chamber and the so-called Thieves' Corridor. [X-ray diffraction of seven samples found only halite, calcite and quartz; electron microscopy of the white crust detected only sodium and chlorine, growing as tiny whiskers; there were no nitrates and no widespread gypsum]{claim=GEO-C907}. So the taste test was right about one thing. The salt on the pyramid's inner walls is common salt.

What the study does not show is that the salt is anomalous. The same paper lists halite as a dominant efflorescence salt at limestone monuments across Egypt — the Menkaure pyramid, the Saqqara pyramid, the White Monastery at Sohag, the Imni tomb at Lisht, and the Sphinx, which is carved from Giza bedrock and which nobody claims was cast. And it cites the geologists Klemm and Klemm for the view that [halite is a primary constituent of the plateau's nummulitic limestone, present within the strata themselves and precipitated from evaporating marine or lagoonal waters when the rock formed]{claim=GEO-C906}. That citation is second-hand — the book has not been read for this case — and no one has compared salt concentrations between pyramid stone and unworked bedrock, or tested whether the salt runs through the body of a block or sits on its skin. But the natron recipe predicts salt in the blocks, and so does ordinary quarrying of a salt-bearing marine limestone. An observation both accounts predict cannot decide between them. The proponents' comparator — cathedrals — is a different rock in a different climate; the comparators that matter are the plateau's own bedrock and its neighbours, and those carry the salt. The comparative claim fails on the record as it stands.

There is a further complication that cuts deeper than the salt. The same study reports that [conservation work inside the pyramid between 1995 and 1997 is undocumented — photographs show that surfaces were cleaned and cavities filled, a sulfur-rich modern fill sits on the chamber wall, and salt that was barely visible in 2022 had spread extensively across the stone two years later]{claim=GEO-C594}. Every surface-salt observation at Giza, including four decades of tasting, is therefore a reading taken at an unknown point in a cleaning cycle whose baseline nobody recorded. That problem is not peculiar to the salt. It hangs over every surface argument at every megalithic site, almost none of which has a complete published restoration history — though that generalisation, unlike the Giza instance, has yet to be audited.

What survives of the salt line is a narrow, cheap question: does unworked Giza and Mokattam bedrock, and the quarry face at Tura, effloresce halite? If yes — as the plateau's geology predicts — the salt argument is finished. If no, the salt becomes an anomaly worth testing in the bulk of the stone rather than on its surface.

## The stone itself

Everything above is circumstantial. The case turns on what the monument stone is actually made of, and here two branches have very different records.

### Egypt: tested, and contradicted

{plate:IMG-GEO-P03}

The pyramid claim is that [some blocks of the Great Pyramid — not the core, but casing, tops, and backing blocks — are cast reconstituted limestone rather than quarried natural stone]{claim=GEO-C020}. Two laboratory results point that way. In 2006 a Drexel University group compared pyramid limestone under electron microscopy with six natural limestones from the area and reported microconstituents combining silicon, calcium, and magnesium “in ratios that do not exist in any of the potential limestone sources”, along with hydrated phases “not known to hydrate in nature” — while conceding that nature “could have — however unlikely — produced all the microstructures examined”. In 2011 an overlapping team applied solid-state NMR to a casing stone from the Bent Pyramid at Dahshur and read it as Tura limestone grains cemented by an amorphous calcium-silicate gel “formed by human intervention”, perhaps with diatomaceous earth added.

Notice the second result quietly changes the recipe. Davidovits proposed an alkali-aluminosilicate geopolymer; the NMR study proposes a lime-pozzolan cement — the chemistry of a mortar, not of a geopolymer. That matters for how the negatives count.

And the negatives are substantial. Four independent petrographic examinations — petrography is the study of stone under a microscope, the geologist's basic tool — every one concluding natural limestone. Folk and Campbell, working across many blocks in the field, report sedimentary bedding, burrows, sharp cross-sections of clams and fragile worm tubes, ripple lamination, and calcite-filled tectonic fractures confined to individual blocks — features that geology produces and moulds do not. Harrell and Penrod examined the “Lauer sample”, the pyramid-interior specimen proponents cite as their showcase, and found natural Mokattam limestone with “no evidence of the special textures and zeolite cement that must exist if the sample is concrete”. Freestone and Middleton ran five techniques on a British Museum casing fragment and found no feature supporting an artificial origin; the cristobalite that Davidovits once treated as a synthetic marker turned out to be opal-CT, a normal sedimentary product. And Jana did the one thing nobody else in this literature has done: he examined casing stones side by side with natural Tura limestone *and* a genuine Davidovits-made geopolymer block — a positive control, the specimen that shows what the signature looks like when it is really there. The silicon-rich spheres highlighted in 2006 appeared in casing stones and natural limestone alike. The geopolymer showed a binder heavily enriched in sodium, potassium, and aluminium that no casing stone showed. The artificial block had a smooth matrix with spherical air voids; the monument stone and the quarry stone shared a grainy texture with pores between the grains.

Weigh the whole. Every examination of Great Pyramid stone by anyone outside the proponent camp reads it as natural, and the one with a positive control shows that the features proponents called artificial occur in undisputed quarry stone, while the features a real binder leaves do not occur in the monument. On this record the claim that some Great Pyramid blocks are cast is contradicted. Two things stop that from being the end of the matter. One is a fight over the samples themselves. Davidovits contends the piece his critics analysed was not the authentic Lauer sample — wrong thickness, missing phosphate coating — though Jana reports finding and mapping that very coating on the piece he received. Egypt's antiquities authority, for its part, states that no sampling permission was ever granted for the 2006 study and that its samples' origin is unknown. The other is the recipe. Jana's decisive negative is a negative for the *alkali* recipe; it does not test the calcium-silicate binder of the 2011 NMR study, which has drawn no published rebuttal and which, at a few per cent by weight, might hide from bulk chemistry. That residue is what a proponent can still honestly point to. It is an objection to the verdict, not evidence against it: nothing in the record has looked for that binder and found it, either.

### The Andes: the branch the case rests on

{plate:IMG-GEO-P04}

At Pumapunku in Bolivia the laboratory evidence is the only kind from a disputed monument that reads as artificial. Two papers from the Davidovits group, published in materials journals in 2019, [report organic matter and microstructural features in Pumapunku stone that the authors argue natural rock should not contain]{claim=GEO-C004}, and on that basis the claim is that [some andesite and red sandstone blocks at Pumapunku and Tiwanaku were geopolymer-cast]{claim=GEO-C021}. Nothing in the record has been aimed directly against those papers — no independent laboratory has re-examined the stone. That makes the claim weakly supported: the only direct evidence on the stone itself points toward casting.

What the papers actually analysed matters. One concerns red sandstone: a sample, PP4, cut from megalithic slab No. 2, a documented architectural block. The other — the one that reports organic matter — concerns andesite, and here the authors' own fuller account of their fieldwork is candid in a way the reader should know. Numerous andesite fragments lie scattered about the site outside the protected monument area; [the andesite sample, PP1, was chosen from that loose debris by its characteristically flat surface]{claim=GEO-C913}, not cut from any identified block. Its attribution to the H-blocks in the plate above is a judgement by appearance, not a documented refit. The authors anticipated the obvious objection — that organic matter in a surface hole of a stone lying in the open is dirt — and answered it by cutting into the fragment: [an interior subsample, PP1C, is reported to show the same carbon- and nitrogen-bearing amorphous matter, including a dark sheet lying beneath two plagioclase crystals]{claim=GEO-C918}. That interior occurrence is the strongest part of the andesite result. It makes simple modern contamination an incomplete explanation, though it is the same team working on the same fragment, and the electron-microscope spectrum that identifies the matter reads elements, not molecules.

Three further admissions, all from the authors. Nitrogen, the element that points to seabird guano as the proposed hardener, cannot be quantified by their equipment; the identification rests on the elemental similarity of the monument matter to guano from the coast at Ilo, and they write that they do not know whether what they see is unreacted guano or the binder itself. No geological andesite was compared with the monument andesite at all — “in the absence of a geological study, we did not know where to look.” And amorphous pockets in Tiwanaku andesite were already noted in an 1892 thin section by the travellers Stübel and Uhle, observers with no stake in any hypothesis — which shows the feature recurs in this stone, and says nothing about whether it is organic or volcanic glass. Radiocarbon dating of the organic matter was announced in 2019 as the next step; no result has been located. A date near AD 600 would strengthen the claim greatly; a modern date would point to contamination.

Beyond the microscope the proponents offer surface morphology — semi-spherical bubbles on the skin of the H-blocks, read as air trapped against a mould, and Protzen and Nair's remark that a hammerstone could never produce the crisp right interior angles of Tiwanaku stonework — together with a llama-caravan guano trade from the coast that they read as exceeding agricultural need, and Cieza de León's report from 1549 that the natives laughed at his question and insisted the stones were made before the Incas reigned. The Protzen quotation is a conventional scholar saying the tooling is unexplained, not that it was cast; the bubbles have not been measured against the natural vesicles of a volcanic rock; the trade argument comes without quantities; and the chronicle, quoted second-hand from a nineteenth-century translation, says nothing about how the stones were made.

So the cautions on the laboratory result stack up. The papers come from one team analysing one sample series. Volcanic rocks host glassy and organic phases naturally, and the criteria for telling natural from artificial were never blind-tested. The andesite fragment has no documented place in the monument and no natural comparator. And there is the Giza precedent: when features of exactly this kind — microstructures read as artificial under the electron microscope — were checked against a genuine geopolymer, they turned out to occur in natural limestone too. Nobody has run that check on andesite.

The standing counter-evidence is a 1971 Bolivian Academy of Sciences study attributing Pumapunku's red sandstones to identifiable natural quarries. It is a provenance study of sandstone set against microscopy of andesite, so the two partly talk past each other — and a quarry match cannot in any case tell dressed stone from stone cast with sand gathered at the same quarry. The proponents' current model is more specific than it used to be, and therefore more checkable. [It holds that the andesite was cast from natural, uncrushed volcanic sand from Cerro Khapia — a material like the Roman pozzolana — carried to and stored at the lakeshore village of Iwawe, where it forms Stratum V of a 2002 excavation, and that the abandoned quadrangular blocks called *piedras cansadas*, “tired stones”, were never used as building material]{claim=GEO-C903}. Both the orthodox account and the proponents agree the andesite comes from Khapia, so quarry geochemistry cannot separate them. A lakeshore deposit, a mountain, and some abandoned blocks can. Reading the excavators' own description of Stratum V is desk work; walking Khapia's outcrops for working faces and dressing debris — or for loose sand and none — is a field season. And the cheapest test of all is to ask what PP1 is: the collection permits, the field photographs, the coordinates, and whether the fragment refits to any catalogued block.

### Can it be done at all?

The one rung of the ladder in decent shape is the humblest: [limestone can be reconstituted into large, hard blocks visually similar to natural stone with materials and temperatures available to ancient builders]{claim=GEO-C012}. Davidovits' institute reports multi-ton demonstration blocks, self-reported and never independently analysed; lime and diatomaceous earth form a calcium-silicate gel at room temperature in the laboratory; and the geopolymer block Jana examined is, after all, a real artificial limestone — distinguishable under the microscope, which is the point, but a stone. Feasibility is not occurrence. But it is not nothing either, and it is the reason this case is a question and not a fantasy.

## The ladder, and why it thins as it climbs

Notice the shape. At the bottom: observations, some solid, most unverified. In the middle: mechanism claims — the ingredients existed, the temperatures were reachable, the chemistry works. At the top: the claim that actually matters, that [at least one major megalithic monument, somewhere, contains man-made cast stone]{claim=GEO-C022}. Each rung is weaker than the one below, and evidence for a lower rung does not automatically climb. Natron in Egypt is established and proves nothing about pyramids. Feasibility is real and proves nothing about history.

The headline claim is existential — *at least one* monument — so it cannot be settled by averaging. Egypt has been tested with binder-aware methods and, in the recipe tested, contradicted. The Andes have been examined by one interested team, on a fragment of uncertain standing, and by nobody else. An existential claim is not refuted by one failed instance, and it is not supported by an untested one. That is why the headline verdict is *unresolved*: not a shrug, but a description of a record in which the decisive test has been run at the wrong site.

## The crux

Here is where the disagreement lives, and it is narrower than either camp usually admits.

The strongest conventional evidence class is provenance matching: monument stone chemically fingerprinted to a quarry. The casting hypothesis's most consequential reply is methodological — [that trace-element quarry-matching methods are blind to hydrogen, carbon, and oxygen, and so cannot by design tell carved quarry stone from stone cast using aggregate gathered at that same quarry]{claim=GEO-C030}. Crushed rock keeps its metallic fingerprint. The narrow point is correct: portable XRF and ICP-MS do not see the light elements a binder is made of, and a quarry match is a quarry match, not a proof of carving. Even at Stonehenge, the West Woods result tells you where the sarsen came from, not how it was shaped. At Khapia it is exactly why the two sides cannot be separated by geochemistry.

But the reply reaches less far than its authors want. The claim lists X-ray diffraction among the blind methods, when XRD reads crystalline phases and is exactly how Folk and Campbell looked for zeolite cement. Fóti's own methods table lists NMR as blind to silicon and oxygen, when solid-state silicon NMR is exactly what the pro-casting Bent Pyramid study used. And the critique does not touch the direct petrography at all. Cast stone needs a binder; binders have signatures — bound water, alkali enrichment, textures geology does not produce. Jana's positive control demonstrates those signatures are plainly visible when present. A methods audit of the provenance literature is worth doing, and it would likely show that some “we found the quarry” conclusions have been stretched into “therefore carved” conclusions the chemistry cannot carry. It would not rescue a monument in which someone has looked directly for a binder and found none.

## What would change our mind

The strongest case for the hypothesis that this record does not answer is this: the revised calcium-silicate binder has never been tested for, and the one monument whose stone reads as artificial in the laboratory has never been examined by anyone but its proponents. The four negative Egyptian studies were built around the alkali recipe, and the one with a positive control used an alkali geopolymer as the control. A cement at five per cent by weight — exactly the kind the 2011 NMR study proposes and the 2010 laboratory work shows is easy to make — could sit inside a casing stone that reads as natural in every one of those tests. At Pumapunku the organic matter lies inside the andesite, under feldspar crystals, not merely on its skin. Nothing in the record rules either out, and the provenance critique means quarry matching cannot rule them out either.

The strongest case against is equally plain: every time monument stone has been examined directly for casting by anyone outside the proponent camp, it has read as natural — down to fossil worm tubes and tectonic fractures; the one Andean fragment that reads otherwise was picked up off the ground by its looks and never compared with the rock it is supposed to differ from; the historical anecdote proponents lean on has no traceable author; and the salt it describes is what the plateau's own rock is reported to shed.

So here is what would move us.

- **Toward casting:** a documented refit of fragment PP1 to a catalogued Pumapunku block, or an independent laboratory reproducing the interior organic matter in a provenance-secure andesite fragment against a natural Khapia control; a radiocarbon date on that organic matter near AD 600; a provenance-secure Egyptian casing stone in which an independent lab finds a calcium-silicate cement absent from a broad natural Tura suite; a blinded paleomagnetic survey of many pyramid blocks, measured against the natural remanence of Mokattam quarry limestone, finding a shared magnetic direction aligned with the present field — something a block that set in place should carry regardless of recipe, and a quarried, rotated block should not; the Iwawe deposit turning out to be a natural andesite sand store dated to the construction period, with no extraction faces on Khapia; a medieval Arabic author who actually reports the salt.
- **Toward carving:** PP1's origin remaining undocumented while its amorphous and organic features are reproduced in undisputed Khapia andesite; a modern radiocarbon date on the organic matter; the sandstone matrix of PP4 reproduced in natural Kimsachata sandstone; a targeted test for a calcium-silicate binder in provenance-secure casing stone returning nothing; halite efflorescing from unworked Giza bedrock, which would retire the salt argument entirely; the Iwawe deposit turning out to be dressing debris or unrelated fill, with quarry faces and carved andesite blocks documented on the way down from Khapia.

This case ends in two different places. On its most famous instance it reaches a conclusion: on the present record, the stone of the Great Pyramid reads as quarried, and the salt on its walls is what the plateau's own rock sheds. On its headline question it does not, because the one monument where the laboratory evidence points the other way has never been examined by anyone without a stake in the answer — and the one andesite sample that points there has yet to be shown to come from the monument at all. The agenda that follows is therefore weighted toward the Andes, and much of it is cheap. Ask what PP1 is, and find a fragment with a catalogue number to test instead. Read the Iwawe excavation report. Walk Khapia's outcrops for quarry faces or for sand. Re-examine the sandstone against a broad natural suite. Design the blinded NMR study with an aged cement as the control, and the blinded paleomagnetic survey that tests set-in-place against quarried without arguing about recipes. Audit which provenance studies can, and cannot, see a binder. Test whether the plateau's bedrock effloresces salt. Finish tracing the salt story through the remaining medieval authors, or drop it. Audit the restoration histories that could account for any surface anomaly — starting with a pyramid interior that was cleaned in the 1990s and nobody wrote down how. Replicate the quarrying rate. Measure the Aswan shafts and read their floors for residues. Re-read the Rekhmire mural with a metallurgist and a chemist in the same room.

The scoop marks at Aswan have waited a very long time for someone to measure them properly. The full agenda, with what each project would tell us, is below.

assessment.synthesis: The thesis (GEO-C022) is existential — at least one monument — so the case cannot be graded by averaging and must be taken branch by branch. The Egyptian branch (GEO-C020) is the only one tested with binder-aware methods on monument stone and it is contradicted: GEO-E018 (in-situ sedimentary bedding, burrows, fossil cross-sections and block-confined tectonic fractures across many blocks), GEO-E019 (the proponents' showcase Lauer sample reads as natural Mokattam limestone with no zeolite cement), GEO-E021 (an independent multi-technique study of a museum casing fragment finds natural limestone and opal-CT rather than synthetic cristobalite), and above all GEO-E020, whose genuine Davidovits-made positive control shows that a real alkali-aluminosilicate binder is plainly visible when present — Na+K and Al enrichment, smooth matrix with air voids — and absent from every casing stone examined, while the Si-rich spheres of GEO-E012 occur in natural limestone too. Against these stand GEO-E012 (contested provenance; features later matched in natural stone) and GEO-E017 (one Bent Pyramid casing stone read by NMR as Tura grains in a calcium-silicate gel; Barsoum co-author; no rebuttal). GEO-E017 is the surviving objection: its C–S–H binder lies outside GEO-E020's alkali-specific negative and GEO-E022 shows the chemistry is feasible, but no record has looked for that binder and found it, so it qualifies the confidence of the negative rather than supplying support. The salt line adds nothing: the medieval report (GEO-C003) is carried only by an uncited proponent page (GEO-E029) and is absent from al-Suyūṭī's compilation of the breach accounts (GEO-E027); the modern salt is confirmed as halite (GEO-E030) but halite effloresces at the carved-bedrock Sphinx and other Egyptian limestone sites (GEO-E031) and is reported, second-hand via Klemm & Klemm, as a primary constituent of Giza limestone (GEO-E032), while undocumented 1990s cleaning leaves every surface observation without a baseline (GEO-E034); GEO-E033 therefore removes the salt as support for GEO-C020 without testing any block. The Andean branch (GEO-C021) is weakly supported, and the ledger now shows exactly how weak. The two 2019 papers are one on red sandstone from slab No. 2 (GEO-E006, sample PP4) and one on andesite (GEO-E007) whose sample PP1 was picked by its flat surface from loose debris outside the protected monument area (GEO-E057), analysed with no natural andesite comparator (GEO-E060), with nitrogen only semi-quantitative and the authors unable to say whether the organic matter is unreacted guano or a binder (GEO-E059). An interior subsample PP1C showing the same carbon- and nitrogen-bearing matter beneath plagioclase (GEO-E058) is the strongest part of the result and makes simple surface dirt an incomplete explanation, but it is the same team and the same fragment, and EDS reads elements, not molecules. The promised radiocarbon date has not been located (GEO-E066); Stübel & Uhle saw amorphous nests in monument andesite in 1892 (GEO-E061), which shows the feature recurs and settles nothing about its nature; surface bubbles and the Protzen quotation (GEO-E062) and the 2020 restatement (GEO-E036) carry no independent weight. The only negative record, GEO-E008, is a 1971 provenance study of sandstone that cannot in principle exclude same-quarry aggregate. So the branch has positive records from one interested team on stone of contested identity and no independent negative: that is weakly_supported, not unresolved and not mixed. The proponents' 2020 model (GEO-E035) makes the branch checkable at Iwawe and Khapia without touching a monument. The methods critique (GEO-C030, GEO-E024) holds in its narrow form — PXRF and ICP-MS are blind to H, C and O, which legitimately limits GEO-E009 and any quarry-match reasoning — but it wrongly lists XRD as blind and does not reach binder-aware petrography. The Aswan material (GEO-E001, GEO-E002, GEO-E003, GEO-E005, GEO-E045) bears on the completeness of the pounding orthodoxy, not on casting. Why the case is unresolved rather than contradicted, mixed or weakly supported: an existential claim is not refuted by one contradicted instance when the other instance has no independent negative record at all; Egypt-negative and Andes-untested is not an evidential collision but a gap; and a single non-independent positive of a type already shown non-diagnostic at Giza does not move the prior. The decisive test has been run at the wrong site. The single evidence record whose removal would most change the case verdict is GEO-E020: without its positive control the Egyptian branch would be two supportive and three negative studies with no demonstration that a casting signature is detectable at all, GEO-C020 would drift toward mixed, GEO-C030 would stand unanswered against the petrography, and the case would move toward mixed. Second is GEO-E058: without the interior occurrence the andesite result would be a surface reading on a loose surface find, and GEO-C021 would fall toward unresolved.
assessment.steelman: The revised calcium-silicate binder has never been tested for, and the only monument whose stone reads as artificial in the laboratory has never been examined by anyone but its proponents. Every negative Egyptian study was built around Davidovits' alkali-aluminosilicate recipe; the one with a positive control (GEO-E020) used an alkali geopolymer as that control and its author concedes a binder at about 5 wt% might not register in bulk chemistry. GEO-E017 reports solid-state ²⁹Si/²⁷Al/⁴³Ca NMR on a Bent Pyramid casing stone reading as Tura grains cemented by an amorphous calcium-silicate gel, with no published rebuttal; GEO-E022 shows lime plus diatomaceous earth forms exactly such a gel at room temperature from materials plausibly available in Egypt; GEO-E012 reports Si–Ca–Mg ratios absent from all six candidate quarries and hydrated phases not known to hydrate in nature, and those specific ratios have not been reproduced in natural stone by any record here. At Pumapunku, GEO-E007 reports organic matter inside dense andesite in a peer-reviewed materials journal; the authors anticipated the surface-contamination objection and cut into the fragment, finding the same carbon- and nitrogen-bearing matter beneath plagioclase crystals in the interior (GEO-E058) — dirt does not lie under feldspar; the guano-trade record (GEO-E063) supplies a documented supply route for the proposed hardener; and no independent analysis, blind comparison or dedicated rebuttal exists, GEO-E008 predating the analytical era and concerning a different lithology. The sandstone paper (GEO-E006) concerns a sample cut from a documented architectural slab, so the branch does not rest on the loose fragment alone. Add the proponents' honest scope restriction in Egypt (casing, tops and backing blocks only, GEO-E023), the valid narrow form of GEO-C030 (a quarry match cannot see a binder, which at Khapia both sides concede), and the fact that the halite the natron recipe predicts is present (GEO-E030) with no bulk-versus-surface test run, and a proponent can say without error that the negative literature refuted the 1980s recipe and then stopped, while the Andean positive has simply never been answered.
assessment.whatIsClaimed: At least one major megalithic monument contains man-made cast stone: blocks produced on site by binding processed mineral inputs (geopolymer, natron/waterglass, lime-pozzolan, or organo-mineral chemistry) rather than by carving natural rock alone. The two concrete instances are casing and backing blocks of the Great Pyramid and the andesite and red sandstone blocks of Pumapunku/Tiwanaku.
assessment.whereDisagreementLives: Not over whether anomalies exist — a measured quarrying rate, halite on the pyramid's inner walls, proponent SEM and NMR findings — and not over the salt, which both accounts predict once halite is native to Giza limestone and which fails as a discriminator on the present record. The Egyptian instance is contradicted on the record as tested; the residual disagreement there is whether the negative petrography, built around an alkali recipe, also excludes the calcium-silicate binder the pro-casting side has moved to, and whether the disputed samples were the right physical objects. The live disagreement is Andean and now has two parts: whether the andesite fragment PP1 — a loose surface find chosen by appearance, never refitted to a block and never compared with natural Khapia andesite — is monument stone at all, and whether the organic and amorphous matter one team reports in it and in the slab No. 2 sandstone would survive an independent, blinded comparison against natural rock, the same audit that at Giza turned claimed casting signatures into ordinary geology; and, at the raw-material end, whether Cerro Khapia yielded dressed blocks or natural sand.
assessment.whatWouldSettleIt: For the Andes, where the case verdict now turns: establish what PP1 is (permits, photographs, coordinates, attempted refit) and test a fragment with an object number independently against a Khapia andesite control, with criteria fixed in advance; locate or run the radiocarbon date on the andesite organic matter; a desk check of the Iwawe Stratum V deposit and the piedras cansadas against the excavators' own descriptions; a survey of Cerro Khapia for extraction faces versus natural sand; and an independent re-analysis of the slab No. 2 sandstone against a broad Kimsachata/Kallamarka suite. For Egypt: blinded multinuclear NMR of provenance-secure casing stone against a stratified natural Tura/Dahshur/Giza suite with aged C–S–H controls; and a blinded paleomagnetic survey of many blocks against a Mokattam natural-limestone remanence baseline, which tests set-in-place versus quarried-and-rotated regardless of recipe. For the salt: XRD of efflorescence on unworked Giza/Mokattam bedrock and Tura quarry faces, which would close the line if positive; and the remaining medieval authors for the al-Maʾmūn report. Either direction is decisive for the specific monument.
assessment.bestConventionalExplanation: Quarrying, carving, and transport with well-attested means: dolerite pounders sourced from dykes within the Aswan granitoids and copper tools, fire-setting, ramps, sledges, levers, and large organized labor forces. This is supported by unfinished monuments abandoned mid-carve at quarries, tool marks and tool-production quarries at extraction sites, worker settlements, radiocarbon dates on construction-context organics, experimental carving, and geochemical provenance matching such as Stone 58 to West Woods. Direct petrography of pyramid stone shows sedimentary bedding, fossils, and tectonic fractures that moulds do not produce, and a genuine geopolymer control shows what a binder looks like when present. Salt on interior walls is halite, which effloresces at the carved-bedrock Sphinx and other Egyptian limestone sites and is reported as a primary sedimentary constituent of Giza limestone, mobilised by humidity and visitor-driven condensation. Slow measured pounding rates imply more labour or supplementary techniques, not manufacture. At Pumapunku, the andesite comes from Cerro Khapia as dressed blocks, the sandstone from identified quarries; the amorphous pockets in the andesite are natural volcanic glass already noted in 1892, and the organic matter in a loose fragment lying in the open is contamination or natural infiltration along microcracks — the loose fragment PP1 has no demonstrated connection to any architectural block. The account's gaps are quantitative, not existential.

components.label: Egyptian branch: Great Pyramid casing, backing and top blocks (GEO-C020)
components.note: Four petrographic studies read the stone as natural, one with a genuine geopolymer positive control; the surviving objection is the untested calcium-silicate binder of GEO-E017 and the sample-identity dispute.

components.label: Andean branch: Pumapunku/Tiwanaku andesite and sandstone (GEO-C021, GEO-C004, GEO-C913, GEO-C918, GEO-C903)
components.note: The only monument stone that reads as artificial in the laboratory, but one team, one sample series, an andesite fragment of undocumented standing, no natural comparator and no independent re-examination; checkable at Iwawe and Khapia.

components.label: Feasibility and ingredients (GEO-C012, GEO-C010, GEO-C011, GEO-C013)
components.note: Natron supply established and artificial limestone demonstrably makeable; the fire-pit discovery story is one anecdote. Feasibility is not occurrence.

components.label: The salt line: medieval report and modern halite (GEO-C003, GEO-C506, GEO-C907, GEO-C906, GEO-C594)
components.note: The halite is real but effloresces at carved-bedrock sites and is reported native to Giza limestone; the al-Maʾmūn salt report has no traceable author; undocumented 1990s cleaning removes any surface baseline.

components.label: Methods critique of quarry-matching (GEO-C030)
components.note: Correct that PXRF and ICP-MS cannot see a binder; wrong to list XRD and NMR as blind; does not reach direct binder-aware petrography.

components.label: Aswan quarrying rate and quarry features (GEO-C001, GEO-C002, GEO-C006, GEO-C502, GEO-C005)
components.note: One well-supported measurement stresses the pounding-only timeline; the tourist anecdote, shaft geometry, Engelbach characterisation and Rekhmire reading are unverified, and pounders are shown to be locally quarried. None of it is evidence of casting.

researchPriority.reason: The tests that would move the case verdict are cheap and decisive — a records request and refit attempt for PP1, a desk read of the Iwawe excavation report, a field walk of Khapia's outcrops, a blinded re-analysis with natural controls — and no funder has yet paid for any of them. Against that, the branch already tested with adequate methods came out contradicted, the only positive laboratory record is from one interested team on a fragment of undocumented standing, and the prior for the thesis is correspondingly low; the value is in closing a long-open question at small cost, not in a likely reversal.

claimAssessments.reasoning: Existential thesis graded branch by branch. Egypt is contradicted by GEO-E018, GEO-E019, GEO-E020 and GEO-E021 against GEO-E012 and GEO-E017. The Andes are weakly supported by GEO-E006, GEO-E007 and GEO-E058 from one team, now heavily qualified by GEO-E057, GEO-E059 and GEO-E060, with no independent negative (GEO-E008 is a sandstone provenance study). GEO-E009 undermines only the Stonehenge instance and, per GEO-C030's narrow form, cannot exclude same-quarry aggregate. An existential claim is neither refuted by one contradicted instance nor supported by an untested one; the honest description is a gap, not a collision.

treatment.plainLanguage: Somewhere in the world, at least one great monument is built partly of stone that was made rather than quarried.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: This is the thesis itself; every other claim is graded by how much it moves this one. The alternatives it competes with are total (all monument stone is natural) and its truth would require only one clean instance.
treatment.strongestObjection: Every time monument stone has been examined directly for a binder by anyone outside the proponent camp it has read as natural, and the one positive laboratory result comes from the proponents on a fragment never shown to be part of the monument and never compared with the rock it supposedly differs from.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: An independent laboratory reproducing interior organic matter or a binder phase in a provenance-secure Pumapunku fragment against a natural Khapia control, with criteria fixed in advance — toward supported.
A calcium-silicate binder found by blinded NMR in provenance-secure casing stone and absent from a broad natural Tura suite — toward supported.

PP1's origin remaining undocumented and its features reproduced in natural Khapia andesite, together with the slab No. 2 sandstone matrix reproduced in natural Kimsachata sandstone — toward contradicted.
Documented Khapia quarry faces with dressing debris and carved andesite ashlars in transit, with Iwawe Stratum V shown to be tephra or dressing debris — toward contradicted.

claimAssessments.reasoning: GEO-E018 (macro-scale sedimentary and tectonic features across many blocks), GEO-E019 (the Lauer sample is natural Mokattam limestone, no zeolite cement), GEO-E021 (independent multi-technique museum fragment: natural, opal-CT not synthetic cristobalite) and GEO-E020 (positive control shows a real alkali binder is visible when present and absent from every casing stone; the Si-rich spheres of GEO-E012 occur in natural stone) outweigh GEO-E012 (contested provenance) and GEO-E017 (one stone, Barsoum co-author, interpretive step from spectra). GEO-E022 shows feasibility only. GEO-E033 removes the salt as support. Confidence is moderate rather than high because the negatives test the alkali recipe and GEO-E017's C–S–H binder has not been looked for, and because the sample-identity dispute on the Lauer piece is a genuine factual disagreement.

treatment.plainLanguage: Some of the Great Pyramid's outer and backing blocks were poured as a kind of concrete rather than cut from quarries.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: The most tested instance of the thesis; a clean positive here would establish GEO-C022 outright, and its contradiction is the strongest single reason the case verdict is not higher.
treatment.strongestObjection: The negative studies were designed around Davidovits' alkali recipe; the calcium-silicate gel proposed by GEO-E017, at a few weight per cent, has never been tested for in casing stone and could read as natural in every method used, and Davidovits disputes that the piece his critics analysed was the true Lauer sample.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Blinded multinuclear NMR (GEO-R017) finding a −84 ppm C–S–H shoulder in provenance-secure casing stone and in no natural Tura/Dahshur/Giza sample, with aged C–S–H controls — toward mixed or supported.
A blinded paleomagnetic survey (GEO-R011) of many blocks showing a shared present-field direction absent from the natural Mokattam baseline — toward mixed.
The same NMR test reproducing the Bent Pyramid shoulder in natural quarry stone — toward contradicted with high confidence.

claimAssessments.reasoning: Positive records on the stone itself: GEO-E006 (sandstone PP4 from slab No. 2), GEO-E007 with GEO-E058 (andesite PP1 and its interior subsample), GEO-E062 (unmeasured bubbles, Protzen quotation) and GEO-E036 (restatement). Qualifiers: GEO-E057 (PP1 is a loose surface find chosen by appearance), GEO-E060 (no natural andesite comparator), GEO-E059 (nitrogen semi-quantitative; guano versus binder unresolved), GEO-E061 (amorphous nests seen in 1892). Negative: GEO-E008, a 1971 sandstone provenance study that cannot exclude same-quarry aggregate. All positives are one team and one sample series, and are of the SEM-microstructure type that GEO-E020 found non-diagnostic at Giza. The claim is weakly supported rather than unresolved because the only direct records on the stone point one way and no independent negative exists; it is not more than weakly supported because none of those records is independent or controlled.

treatment.plainLanguage: Some of the famous precision-cut blocks at Pumapunku were moulded from a mineral paste rather than carved.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: The instance on which the case verdict now turns: if this were independently confirmed GEO-C022 would be established; if PP1 proved to be non-monument debris and the sandstone matrix natural, the case would fall to contradicted.
treatment.strongestObjection: The andesite evidence is a loose fragment picked off the ground by its looks, analysed by the proponents with no natural andesite to compare it to, using a technique that reads elements not molecules; features of exactly this type were shown at Giza to occur in natural stone once a positive control was run.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A documented refit of PP1 to a catalogued block, or a provenance-secure fragment reproducing the interior organic matter in an independent laboratory against a Khapia control (GEO-R016) — toward provisionally supported.
A radiocarbon date near AD 600 on the andesite organic matter — toward supported; a modern date — toward contradicted.
The slab No. 2 sandstone matrix reproduced in a broad natural Kimsachata/Kallamarka suite (GEO-R019), and the andesite features reproduced in Khapia outcrop andesite — toward contradicted.
Documented Khapia quarry faces and carved ashlars in transit (GEO-R012, GEO-R009) — toward contradicted.

claimAssessments.reasoning: As a claim about what was published it is straightforwardly true: GEO-E007 reports organic matter in Pumapunku andesite read as a binder residue, and GEO-E058 the interior occurrence. GEO-E006's corrected title shows the companion paper concerns red sandstone (PP4), so only one published paper is about andesite. The credibility of the report is not in doubt; its diagnosticity is: GEO-E057 (loose fragment, no identified block), GEO-E060 (no geological comparator), GEO-E059 (EDS-only, nitrogen semi-quantitative, guano versus binder unresolved), GEO-E061 (amorphous matter recurs in monument andesite since 1892), GEO-E066 (no radiocarbon date located).

treatment.plainLanguage: Scientists have published microscope results saying Pumapunku's andesite contains organic material and textures that natural volcanic rock should not have.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: A credible observation that is weak evidence for the thesis: the andesite result rests on one loose fragment of undocumented standing, without a natural andesite control, identified by elemental spectra alone, from the hypothesis's own proponents. The interior subsample is its strongest part.
treatment.strongestObjection: The sample was not taken from an identified architectural block, no natural Khapia andesite was examined alongside it, and volcanic rocks host amorphous glassy phases naturally — the features have never been shown absent from the parent rock.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Independent SEM/EDS and organic analysis of a provenance-secure fragment against a Khapia andesite control reproducing the interior organic matter — the observation becomes diagnostic.
The same features found in outcrop andesite from Khapia — the observation loses its bearing on casting.
A published radiocarbon result on the organic matter, in either direction.

claimAssessments.reasoning: The analysts' own account (GEO-E057) states that numerous andesite fragments lie outside the protected monument area and that PP1 A and B came from the fresh broken part of a fragment on the ground, chosen by its characteristically flat surface. The peer-reviewed statement of the same context was not shown, but this is the authors' fuller description of their own sampling and there is nothing in the ledger against it.

treatment.plainLanguage: The andesite piece whose analysis is the case's main Andean evidence was picked up from loose rubble outside the protected area because it looked like monument stone, not cut from a known block.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Caps the weight of GEO-C004 and GEO-C021: the andesite result is an observation about a surface find attributed to the monument by appearance. It does not show the fragment is not monument stone; it shows nobody has demonstrated that it is.
treatment.strongestObjection: A flat dressed surface is a reasonable marker of architectural stone at a site strewn with broken blocks, and lying outside the protected perimeter does not exclude the fragment being from a monument block displaced by collapse or looting.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Collection permits, field photographs, coordinates or a physical refit tying PP1 to a catalogued block — the observation's limiting force disappears.
The Ceramics International text shown and found to describe a different, documented sampling context — the claim would need revision.

claimAssessments.reasoning: GEO-E058 records the analysts' statement that a smaller sample PP1C cut from the interior of PP1A showed several spots with the same EDS spectrum (C, N, Na, Mg, Al, Si, P, S, Cl, K, Ca), including a dark sheet lying beneath two plagioclase crystals. The claim is about what the analysts report, and they do report it; confidence is moderate because the source is the team's self-published transcript rather than the peer-reviewed paper, and the observation itself is uncorroborated.

treatment.plainLanguage: When the researchers cut into the andesite fragment, they say they found the same carbon- and nitrogen-rich material inside it, under mineral crystals, not just on the surface.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: The strongest part of the Andean result: an interior occurrence makes simple modern surface dirt an incomplete explanation. It remains one team on one fragment of undocumented origin, read by elemental spectra that cannot identify the compound, with no natural control; infiltration of organics along microcracks in a fragment that lay in the open is not excluded — a point that rests on priors rather than any record.
treatment.strongestObjection: Same team, same fragment, EDS only; the fragment's own history is unknown, and natural volcanic glass already appears as amorphous pockets in this stone (GEO-E061), so an interior amorphous phase is expected on the natural account and only its organic character is at issue.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Independent reproduction of interior C/N-bearing matter in a provenance-secure fragment with molecular characterisation (e.g. FTIR, Raman, isotopes) — strongly toward casting.
A radiocarbon date on the matter: ancient supports a binder, modern indicates contamination.
Interior amorphous matter in Khapia outcrop andesite showing the same spectrum — retires the observation.

claimAssessments.reasoning: A description of the proponents' own model, stated directly in the abstract of GEO-E035: natural, uncrushed andesite sand from Cerro Khapia, stored at Iwawe as Stratum V of Isbell & Burkholder 2002, with the piedras cansadas not used as building material. GEO-E036 confirms continuity with Parts I–III.

treatment.plainLanguage: The casting theory's current version says the builders used natural volcanic sand from a nearby mountain, stockpiled at a lakeshore village, and never used the abandoned blocks lying around the lake.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Diagnostic not because it is true but because it is checkable: it names a deposit and a class of objects whose examination could confirm or retire the Andean raw-material story without touching a monument, and it explains why quarry geochemistry alone cannot decide the branch.
treatment.strongestObjection: Abstract only; the excavators' own description of Stratum V and the piedras cansadas has not been read, and the model concedes no compositional test yet ties the deposit to Khapia or to monument stone.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Isbell & Burkholder 2002 describing Stratum V as tephra or dressing debris — the model's aggregate source fails.
A compositional match of Stratum V to loose Khapia sand, dated to the construction period, with no extraction faces on Khapia — the model gains a real prediction.

claimAssessments.reasoning: GEO-E024 correctly states that PXRF and ICP-MS cannot detect H, C or O and that a quarry match cannot see a binder; GEO-E009 shows what such a match does and does not establish; GEO-E035 shows both sides now accept a Khapia origin, making the narrow point live. But the claim lists XRD among the blind methods, which is wrong (GEO-E018 used XRD to look for zeolite cement), and GEO-E020 demonstrates that binder-aware petrography sees what quarry chemistry cannot, so the critique does not reach the direct Egyptian negatives.

treatment.plainLanguage: Matching a stone's chemical fingerprint to a quarry cannot tell you whether it was carved there or made from that quarry's crushed rock, because the fingerprinting methods cannot see the elements a binder is made of.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Limits how much the strongest conventional evidence class constrains the thesis; it does not supply support for casting and does not answer the petrography.
treatment.strongestObjection: Cast stone needs a binder and binders leave signatures — alkali enrichment, textures, bound water — that binder-aware microscopy detects when present, as GEO-E020's positive control shows; the critique is aimed at the wrong studies.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A methods audit (GEO-R003) showing provenance conclusions routinely stretched to 'therefore carved' — strengthens the narrow form.
A demonstration that a low-percentage C–S–H or organo-mineral binder escapes standard petrography as well — broadens the claim's reach.
Correction of the XRD/NMR errors in the claim as stated — the claim would need narrowing.

claimAssessments.reasoning: GEO-E013 (self-reported demonstration blocks), GEO-E022 (lime plus diatomaceous earth forms C–S–H at room temperature), and GEO-E020's use of a genuine Davidovits geopolymeric limestone as a positive control together show artificial limestone can be made; GEO-E012 shows the features proponents attribute to it exist somewhere. No independent analysis of a demonstration block exists, and 'large' has been shown only by self-report.

treatment.plainLanguage: It is possible to make hard, natural-looking limestone blocks from limestone rubble and simple chemistry that ancient people could have had.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: A necessary condition for the thesis, not evidence of it; it is why the case is a question rather than a fantasy, and it explains nothing about any monument.
treatment.strongestObjection: Modern laboratory production says nothing about ancient practice, and the multi-ton blocks are self-reported by the proponent organisation.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Independent analysis of a demonstration block confirming size, hardness and recipe — toward well supported.
Failure to reproduce a hard, large block from the stated ancient-feasible inputs — toward weakly supported.

claimAssessments.reasoning: The only ledger record is GEO-E016, a proponent's citation of early glassmaking as a temperature precedent, graded weak; the verdict leans on the general knowledge that ancient metallurgy and glassmaking reached such temperatures, which is a prior rather than a ledger record.

treatment.plainLanguage: Ancient furnaces could reach the roughly 850 °C needed for natron to attack silica.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: A feasibility rung; crucible-scale heat is not industrial-scale processing, and it says nothing about whether the chemistry was applied to stone.
treatment.strongestObjection: Reaching a temperature in a crucible is far from sustaining it across the volumes casting-scale production would demand.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Verified dating and temperature estimates for pre-pyramid glassmaking — toward well supported.
Evidence that sustained large-volume alkali melting was impossible with attested Egyptian furnaces — toward contradicted for the scale claimed.

claimAssessments.reasoning: GEO-E010 (strong, mainstream) identifies Wadi el Natrun and al-Barnuj as the ancient natron sources with a documented 7th–9th-century decline; GEO-E011 supplies the compositional tool behind the timeline.

treatment.plainLanguage: Egypt had huge natural deposits of natron, mined since antiquity, whose supply collapsed in the early medieval period.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Ingredient availability only; the papers concern glass and faience and say nothing about stone.
treatment.strongestObjection: Natron's documented use is in glass, faience and mummification; nothing ties it to stonemaking.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Nothing on the ledger threatens the claim; it would matter more only if natron residues were found in monument stone.

claimAssessments.reasoning: GEO-E015 is one unattributed anecdote from a proponent text, never replicated.

treatment.plainLanguage: Stone-like material can form by accident in long-used campfire pits, which might be how people first discovered stone-making.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: A discovery story; its failure would not touch the thesis and its success would only make the origin narrative more plausible.
treatment.strongestObjection: An unattributed anecdote with no controlled observation.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Controlled multi-month fire-pit cycles (GEO-R007) producing structurally stone-like material — toward supported.
The same cycles producing only friable ash — toward contradicted.

claimAssessments.reasoning: GEO-E001 is a peer-reviewed photogrammetric measurement (216 cm³/h at 85 strikes/min) from a single team; GEO-E002 contextualises the older basis it replaces. No replication yet.

treatment.plainLanguage: When measured properly, hammering granite with a dolerite ball removes only about a cup of rock per hour.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Stresses the pounding-only timeline for the Aswan obelisk; fire-setting, chisels or more labour absorb the shortfall without any casting, so it does not discriminate the thesis from the alternatives.
treatment.strongestObjection: Single study; skilled crews with maintained tools and fire-setting may far outperform the experimental protocol.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Independent replication with sensitivity analysis (GEO-R002) — confirms or dissolves the anomaly.
Documented fire-setting at the obelisk quarry quantified against the removal volume — retires the anomaly's force.

claimAssessments.reasoning: GEO-E003 is an unquantified proponent anecdote; GEO-E002 is context. No survey of attempts or wear exists.

treatment.plainLanguage: Tourists have hammered the test block at Aswan for decades without producing a single scoop mark.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Even if true it shows that untrained visitors in minutes cannot do what crews did in months; it bears on technique, not on casting.
treatment.strongestObjection: Nobody has counted attempts, measured effort or examined the block; the null result is expected under the conventional account for casual strikes.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A documented survey of the test block's wear and a controlled attempt by trained workers over hours — either direction.

claimAssessments.reasoning: GEO-E005 is a proponent description; shaft dimensions and the biomechanical claim are untested. The conventional test-shaft reading is recorded in the plate description but not as a ledger record.

treatment.plainLanguage: Deep, narrow holes beside the Aswan obelisk seem too tight for anyone to swing a hammer stone at the bottom.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Unmeasured conjecture either way; geometry and residues would decide between prospecting pits and processing vessels.
treatment.strongestObjection: Engelbach read them as test shafts sunk before the trench was cut, and no survey has recorded their actual dimensions or floors.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A measured survey with residue sampling (GEO-R013): silicate or alkali residues and water-tight walls — toward the casting reading; pounded floors and fissure-following courses — retires the anomaly.

claimAssessments.reasoning: GEO-E002 records the characterisation as Fóti's and unverified against the 1922 monograph; the same author's characterisations of three other sources differ from the originals (SRC-FOTI-2024 reliability notes).

treatment.plainLanguage: The century-old textbook account of how the Aswan granite was pounded out rests on one man's one-hour experiment and some rough guesses.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: If accurate it weakens the historical basis of the pounding orthodoxy; it says nothing about casting, and Engelbach himself did not think the trench was cut by hand pounding alone.
treatment.strongestObjection: The characterisation has not been checked against the monograph, and the author characterising it has been found to misstate other sources.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Direct reading of Engelbach §§13–15 confirming or correcting the trial, rate and workforce inference.

claimAssessments.reasoning: GEO-E027: al-Suyūṭī's compilation gives two detailed accounts of the breach with no mention of salt; GEO-E029: the only carrier of the report is an uncited proponent page; GEO-E028: even its date is unsupported. GEO-E004 supports weakly. Confidence is low because other medieval authors remain unread.

treatment.plainLanguage: Medieval accounts of the caliph's break-in are said to describe salt coating the pyramid's inner walls.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Even if a medieval source existed, salt on the walls is predicted by both the natron recipe and quarrying of a salt-bearing marine limestone (GEO-C906), so it would not discriminate.
treatment.strongestObjection: Al-Maqrīzī's full chapter, ʿAbd al-Laṭīf and the Arabic extracts in Vyse have not been read; a single located passage would revive the report.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A medieval Arabic author actually reporting salt in the chambers (GEO-R001) — toward supported.
The remaining authors read with no salt — toward contradicted with high confidence.

claimAssessments.reasoning: The presence component holds (GEO-E030: efflorescence is halite); the comparative component fails: GEO-E031 documents halite efflorescence at the carved-bedrock Sphinx and other Egyptian limestone sites, GEO-E032 reports halite as a primary constituent of Giza limestone (second-hand), and GEO-E026's cathedral comparator is the wrong control. GEO-E034 removes any surface baseline.

treatment.plainLanguage: The pyramid's stones are salty in a way that other natural limestone monuments are not.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Both accounts predict salt in the blocks, so even a confirmed anomaly would be weak; on the record the anomaly itself fails.
treatment.strongestObjection: No one has measured salt concentrations in unworked Giza bedrock against pyramid stone, or tested bulk versus surface distribution; the Klemm & Klemm statement is cited second-hand.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: XRD of efflorescence on unworked Giza/Mokattam bedrock and Tura faces (GEO-R010) finding no halite — the salt becomes a real anomaly.
The same test finding halite — the line closes.

claimAssessments.reasoning: GEO-E030: XRD of seven samples found only halite, calcite and quartz; SEM-EDX of the crust found only Na and Cl; no nitrates, no widespread gypsum. Modern instrumentation in a peer-reviewed conservation study.

treatment.plainLanguage: Laboratory analysis confirms the white crust inside the Great Pyramid's chambers is ordinary salt.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Confirms the observation behind the salt argument and takes away nothing from either account: both predict it.
treatment.strongestObjection: Only efflorescence and detached fragments were analysed; bulk distribution in the blocks is untested.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Nothing threatens the observation; its bearing changes only with a bedrock comparator.

claimAssessments.reasoning: GEO-E032 reports the statement as Sessa et al.'s citation of Klemm & Klemm 2010, with detached substrate fragments showing Na and Cl as probable inherent components; the book has not been read and the statement is second-hand.

treatment.plainLanguage: Salt is part of the natural rock of the Giza plateau, laid down when the limestone formed in evaporating seawater.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: If true it dissolves the salt line entirely by making the pyramid's halite expected under quarrying; it bears on nothing else.
treatment.strongestObjection: A second-hand citation in a conservation paper, not a read primary, and no efflorescence survey of unworked bedrock is on the ledger.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Klemm & Klemm 2010 read directly, and Hemeda & Sonbol 2020's bulk XRD of backing limestone — toward established.
Unworked bedrock and quarry faces free of halite — toward contradicted.

claimAssessments.reasoning: GEO-E034 supplies one concrete instance at the most-cited monument — undocumented 1995–97 cleaning and filling inside the Khufu pyramid, a sulfur-rich modern fill, salt re-forming within two years. The general claim about megalithic sites has not been audited.

treatment.plainLanguage: Hardly any ancient site has a full record of modern repairs, so odd surface features may be recent, not ancient.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: A confound that weakens every surface-based argument on both sides — taste tests, bubbles, coatings, veneer appearances — without bearing on the stone's interior.
treatment.strongestObjection: One monument interior is not a survey of megalithic sites; the generalisation rests on an unaudited catalog note.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A restoration-history audit (GEO-R005) at Giza, Tiwanaku, Cusco and Easter Island — toward established if records are as thin as claimed, toward contradicted if full histories exist.

claimAssessments.reasoning: GEO-E014 is a proponent's interpretive argument; conventional Egyptology reads the scene as bronze casting and has not engaged the reinterpretation.

treatment.plainLanguage: A famous Egyptian tomb painting of workers casting metal might instead show large-scale mineral processing.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: An iconographic argument that, even if accepted, would show a process was depicted, not that any monument was cast.
treatment.strongestObjection: The scene's inscriptions and conventional reading as metal casting have not been shown deficient by anyone with Egyptological training.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A joint Egyptology/history-of-technology re-examination (GEO-R008) finding the bronze reading cannot account for the depicted apparatus — toward supported; finding it can — toward contradicted.
